analysis.one_liner: Lets states offer a Medicaid buy-in as a low-cost public health insurance option.
analysis.headline: Ten House Democrats sponsored the bill; it never left committee and received no vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any state open its Medicaid program to residents who don't already have coverage, letting them buy in with premiums capped at 8.5% of household income and eligible for the same tax credits available for private plans [S2] [S3]. It would also raise Medicaid pay for primary care to Medicare rates, guarantee Medicaid coverage of reproductive health care including abortion in every state, and give late-expanding states the same federal money early Medicaid-expansion states got [S2] [S3]. Participation would be optional for each state.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults who fall into the coverage gap or find marketplace and employer plans unaffordable would gain a public option with income-based premiums; women in every state would gain guaranteed Medicaid coverage of reproductive health care, including abortion; and primary care providers would gain higher, guaranteed Medicaid payment rates [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicaid buy-in: residents without other coverage could buy into their state's Medicaid plan starting January 1, 2025, at each state's option, with premiums and cost-sharing allowed only within set limits

Caps family premiums for the buy-in at 8.5% of household income and applies Affordable Care Act cost-sharing limits, with enrollees eligible for the same premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions as marketplace customers
Gives states a 90% federal match for administering the buy-in program, and routes advance premium tax credits to state Medicaid agencies to lower enrollees' premiums
Requires every state's Medicaid program to cover comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care, including abortion services, as a condition of plan approval

Restores and makes permanent a payment floor that guarantees primary care providers at least Medicare-level Medicaid payment rates, expanded to obstetricians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, certified nurse-midwives, and community clinics
Gives states that expand Medicaid late the same enhanced federal matching rates on the same schedule as early expander states, removing the financial penalty for waiting

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the cost of the enhanced matching rates, the 90% administrative match, the primary care pay floor, and a $50 million appropriation for quality measures; in states that opt in, state Medicaid budgets would cover any gap between premium revenue and the cost of care [S2] [S3]. Private insurers and hospitals would face a cheaper public competitor and lower-paying patients in opt-in states [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and state taxpayers, private insurers

drawbacks.text: The federal government would cover 90% of buy-in administrative costs, pay enhanced matching rates to every late-expanding state, guarantee Medicare-level primary care payment rates indefinitely, and appropriate $50 million — a significant open-ended federal cost

Medicaid payment rates are generally lower than private insurance rates, so hospitals and specialists could see thinner margins on newly enrolled patients; the bill excludes emergency department services from the higher primary care floor
Mandating that every state's Medicaid program cover abortion services as a condition of federal plan approval is a major and contested expansion that overrules state-level restrictions
Because adoption is optional state by state, the public option would be available only where states choose to offer it, leaving coverage gaps elsewhere

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who cannot afford marketplace plans or whose employer coverage is unaffordable, a Medicaid buy-in with premiums capped at 8.5% of income and access to tax credits would be a substantial benefit at low personal cost. The honest costs are real: open-ended federal spending on matching rates and provider pay increases, lower payment rates that some providers may not accept, and a contested national mandate on abortion coverage that would almost certainly draw legal and political resistance. The state-by-state opt-in design softens the mandate but also limits how many people would actually benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and a health subcommittee from March 2024 until the Congress ended in January 2025, and no committee or floor vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Kim Schrier introduced the State Public Option Act on March 22, 2024, joined by nine Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans

The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and it was then sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where it remained without a markup or vote
The bill's last recorded action was a second subcommittee referral on December 17, 2024; no committee or floor vote ever took place before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, hospitals, and anyone opposed to a lower-priced public insurance competitor are better off, because the bill never advanced and would have competed directly with private marketplace plans and routed new premium revenue through Medicaid. States with abortion restrictions also avoided a federal mandate to cover abortion services in Medicaid.

for.name: Rep. Kim Schrier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a state Medicaid buy-in public option and recruited nine Democratic cosponsors

for.name: Nine House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. McCollum, Swalwell, Cohen, Tonko, Norton, Matsui, Omar, Phillips, and Moore
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican joined

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction, sent it to the Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received a concurrent referral over its jurisdiction (tax credits and Medicare payment provisions) and took no action on the bill

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling committee calendars and floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: Allowed no committee or floor action on any of the public-option bills referred to its committees during the 118th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill also died in committees controlled by the House Republican majority, so the fight followed party lines entirely.

industries.note: A Medicaid buy-in with income-capped premiums and ACA tax credits would compete directly with marketplace plans and employer coverage, drawing away customers paying higher private premiums. Insurers benefit from the bill's failure, which keeps a cheaper public alternative off the table.

The bill lets states enroll buy-in participants through managed care contracts, so a state public option would still route many enrollees through private Medicaid plans and their capitation payments. The companies gain new enrollees but face the public plan as a competitor in the individual market.

Newly covered patients mean fewer unpaid bills, but Medicaid generally pays less than private insurance, so hospitals and specialists would earn less on buy-in patients. The bill also bars the higher primary care payment floor from applying to emergency department services.

industries.industry: Primary care physicians, nurse practitioners, and community clinics
industries.note: The bill revives and makes permanent a rule requiring Medicaid to pay primary care providers at Medicare rates, and extends it to OB/GYNs, advance practice clinicians, rural health clinics, and federally qualified health centers. Better Medicaid pay supports access for low-income patients.

The bill commits the federal government to a 90% share of buy-in administrative costs, enhanced matching rates for every late-expanding state, Medicare-level primary care rates, and a $50 million appropriation. These are open-ended federal spending commitments without an offset in the bill.
